newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq again complains over delay in food deliveries.
newsitem.headline: Iraq again complains over delay in food deliveries.

text.p: Iraq's U.N. envoy lobbied non-aligned Security Council members on Friday for a speed-up in approval of contracts to purchase humanitarian goods under an "oil-for-food" deal with the United Nations.

Ambassador Nizar Hamdoon also said he told the group the issue of several hundred missing Kuwaitis and others, dating from Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, should not be linked to lifting of sanctions against his country. The issue was raised by several members during the council's latest 60-day review of sanctions on Monday, when the curbs were again left intact.

"Up till yesterday 240 contracts (for the purchase by Iraq of humanitarian goods) were presented. Only 15 are approved. This is the bottom line," Hamdoon told reporters. "If we will see this coming week more like 60 or 70 contacts approved, we will feel better."

Hamdoon and Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf, who recently visited New York, have complained about delays in the arrival of food, medicine and other goods under a deal that allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy badly needed supplies to help offset effects of sanctions.
The deal went into effect on Dec. 10 and oil sales have gone smoothly but Iraq says none of the food has yet arrived.

Asked about new "points of understanding" recently adopted by the U.N. Iraqi sanctions committee for speeding the handling of contracts for humanitarian purchases, Hamdoon said this was "a step forward, but more things have to be done."
On the missing persons issue, he said this had "been recently politicized by some of my colleagues from Kuwait and from Britain, with an effort to try to link it with the lifting of the sanctions."
"I explained that this is a matter that should not be politicized, it is purely humanitarian," he said. "And secondly, it should not be linked with the sanctions regime."

He said Iraq last month offered to allow the Geneva-based International Committee of the Red Cross to "visit our prisons and camps of detention in Iraq in order to help out with the process of searching for the missing people, which was highly appreciated by the ICRC."

A prime condition for the lifting of sanctions is a report to the Security Council by the U.N. special committee in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction that its nuclear, chemical, biological and ballistic missile potential has been fully accounted for and eliminated.
